senses.gloss:
Virūpākṣa Temple
------------------------------------------
Virūpākṣa is one of the epithets of शिव since he has ‘distorted eyes’ (virūpa = distorted, akṣa = eye), his having three eyes instead of two, itself being the ‘distortion’.
The शिव temple at हम्पि (in the Bellary district of Karnataka) is known as the विरूपाक्ष तेम्प्ले or the Pampāpati Temple. The original temple might have been built in the 11th century A. D. and gradually became a big complex by the 16th century. It was renovated by the emperor Kṛṣṇadevarāya (A. D. 1488-1529) in A. D. 1510).
The temple is situated on the northern bank of the river Tuṅgabhadrā and at the northern end of the famous हम्पि bazaar. Out of the three gopuras (towers) the one at the eastern entrance is the highest. It is estimated to be 50 metres (164 feet) high. It has nine storeys.
There is a large number of small shrines and maṇḍapas (pavilions) in the temple complex.
One of these maṇḍapas contains bas-relief figures. There are also paintings, one of which depicts the scene of अर्जुन (the Pāṇḍava hero) discharging the arrow to hit the eye of the rotating fish—this is known as matsyayantrabhedana—during the स्वयṁवर (See SVAYAṀVARA.) of द्रौपदी, daughter of the king Drupada of the Pāñcāla country. There is also another painting of the sage विद्यारण्य (A. D. 1296-1386) going in a procession (See VIDYĀRAṆYA.). Elsewhere in the temple there is a small shrine dedicated to him.
Regular worship has been going on in the main temple even now.
See HAMPI.

vīrabhāva
(‘heroic attitude’)
------------------------------------------
This is the attitude of the vīrasādhaka who is following the वामाचार mode of sādhana given in the तन्त्रस्.
See under TANTRAS.

Virāj
(‘one who shines in a special way;’ ‘the immense being’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used in the Vedāntic works.
If ईश्वर is the original creator of this world, हिरण्यगर्भ is his first evolute. From him emanates विराज् or Virāṭ. He is the cosmic being having the totality of the gross bodies of the world as his body. He is also called वैश्वानर.
Viśva is his manifestation at the individual level.
Kṛṣṇa declares in the Bhagavadgītā (15.14) that it is he who, as वैश्वानर, digests the ड़ोओद् in the bodies of all living beings.
The Puruṣasūkta (5) declares that Virāṭ was born out of the Ādipuruṣa or the primeval being. The Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad (2.1.4) describes his cosmic form having अग्नि or fire as his head, चन्द्र and सूर्य (the मोओन् and the sun) as his eyes, the dik or the quarters as his ears and so on. He is the antarātmā, the inner Self, of all the living beings.
See also VAIŚVĀNARA.

viruddha
(‘contradictory’)
------------------------------------------
This is a technical term used in न्याय philosophy. It is the second fallacy listed under हेत्वाभास (See HETVĀ-BHĀSA.) which has five such.
In the statement, ‘Air is heavy because it is empty’, the middle term ‘empty’ is contradictory because it disproves the heaviness of air. This is called ‘viruddha’.

Virajāhoma
(‘homa to become free from impurities’)
------------------------------------------
When a person decides to take saṁnyāsadīkṣā—embrace monastic life with certain vows—he has to perform some rites and ceremonies. One of the most important of these is the विरजाहोम.
It is a lengthy ritual. It comprises offering forty oblations in a duly consecrated fire with fuel sticks, cooked rice and ghee. The mantras are the ones given in the Mahānārāyaṇa Upaniṣād (sections 65 and 66).
A typical format of the mantras is like this: ‘May my five prāṇas be purified, may I be light or illumination, free from रजस् and from evil, स्वाहा!’
This is repeated a number of times to include several items such as five senses, the मिन्द्, the intellect, the seed, the thought, the constituents of the body, the several limbs of the body, the five guṇas of the elements, the five kośas or sheaths and so on.

Virāṭa
------------------------------------------
Virāṭa was the king of Matsyadeśa, and his capital was Virāṭanagarī. Sudeṣṇā was his second wife and उत्तरकुमार was his son from her. उत्तरा was his daughter.
When the Pāṇḍavas, after losing the game of dice, were banished, they had to spend twelve years in a forest and the thirteenth year incognito. During this last year, they chose to live in the Virāṭanagarī in disguise, as employees of the king विराट.
Once, Suśarmā, the king of Trigarta, attacked Virāṭanagarī and captured the king विराट. He was liberated by भीम (then known as Valvala working as a cook) as per the command of युधिष्ठिर (then disguised as a recluse, by name Kaṅka).
Immediately after the one year period was over, when the Pāṇḍavas revealed their identity, विराट was happy and offered his daughter उत्तरा in मर्रिअगे to अभिमन्यु, the son of अर्जुन.
Virāṭa joined the Pāṇḍava army in the कुरुक्षेत्र battle, fought for them, but was killed by Droṇa.
Matsyadeśa has now been identified with the area around the modern Jaipur city in Rajasthan.

vīrāsana
(‘heroic posture’)
------------------------------------------
Works on हठयोग like the Gheraṇḍa Saṁhitā and the Haṭhayoga-pradīpikā prescribe several āsanas or yogic postures that help in regaining and retaining good health as also controlling the prāṇic energy.
One such आसन is the वीरासन. In the sitting posture, the left leg is to be folded under the right thigh. The right leg is also folded, keeping the foot on the left thigh.

Vīrabhadra
------------------------------------------
When दक्ष, the प्रजापति, performed a great sacrifice, he did not invite Śiva—his own son-in-law—for the same. सती, शिव’s wife and दक्ष’s daughter, went to attend the sacrifice much against the advice of her husband. दक्ष ignored her and also reviled her husband शिव. Unable to stand the insult, she gave up her body using her yogic powers. When शिव got this news, he was infuriated. He created an ogre from his hair and commanded him to destroy दक्ष’s sacrifice. This ogre was Vīrabhadhra. He was a partial manifestation of रुद्र/Śiva.
Iconographical works show Vīra-bhadra in different ways. He is shown with two arms, four arms or eight arms. Objects shown in his hands are: sword, shield, bow, arrow, trident, skull-cup, goad, antelope, mace and hand-drum. He wears a garland of several heads and rides on a vetāla or a vampire.
Bhadrakālī (his spouse) and दक्ष with the head of a goat in the posture of supplication are shown by his side.
Vīrabhadra is shown in a small shrine in all the temples of शिव. He is also shown in the panels showing the Sapta-mātṛkās (See SAPTAMĀTṚKĀS.).

Virocana
------------------------------------------
According to the Chāndogya Upaniṣad (8.7) विरोचन was the king of the असुरस् (antigods or demons) who went to the teacher प्रजापति to get the knowledge of आत्मन् (the Self). He, with his limited intellect, understood that the physical body itself was the आत्मन् and propagated the same to his flock. Consequently, the असुरस् became gross materialists.
As per the Mahābhārata (Udyogaparva 35) विरोचन was the son of प्रह्लाद and ड़थेर् of बलि. Once he had a disputation with a ब्राह्मण sage Sudhanva about the relative superiority of a ब्राह्मण and a क्षत्त्रिय, but lost it.

Virāṭaparva
------------------------------------------
This is the fourth book of the epic Mahābhārata.
See MAHĀBHĀRATA.
